summary: Jesus comes to Bethany when Lazarus has been dead four days, weeps with the mourners, and calls him out of the tomb: He is the resurrection and the life.
key_insight: John writes, “Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when He heard that he was sick, He stayed two more days” (11:5–6). The delay did not contradict His love; John says it came from it. Jesus was aiming at more than a healing.
story: A man named Lazarus was sick. He lived in Bethany, the village of his sisters Mary and Martha; this was the Mary who would anoint the Lord with fragrant oil and wipe His feet with her hair. The sisters sent word to Jesus: “Lord, behold, he whom You love is sick.” When Jesus heard it, He said, “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”

Jesus loved Martha, her sister and Lazarus. So when He heard that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was two more days. Then He said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.” They reminded Him that the Jews had just tried to stone Him there. Jesus answered that a man who walks in the day does not stumble. Then He said, “Our friend Lazarus sleeps, but I go that I may wake him up.” When they took Him to mean ordinary sleep, He told them plainly, “Lazarus is dead.” He was glad for their sakes that He had not been there, so that they might believe. Thomas, called the Twin, said to the others, “Let us also go, that we may die with Him.”

When Jesus arrived, Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, and many had come out to comfort the sisters. As soon as Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet Him, while Mary stayed in the house. “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever You ask of God, God will give You.”

Jesus said, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha answered, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live. And whoever lives and believes in Me shall never die. Do you believe this?” She said, “Yes, Lord, I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who is to come into the world.”

Martha went and quietly called her sister: “The Teacher has come and is calling for you.” Mary rose quickly and went to Him, and the mourners followed, thinking she was going to the tomb to weep. When she reached Jesus, she fell at His feet and said what her sister had said: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.”

When Jesus saw her weeping, and the mourners weeping with her, He groaned in the spirit and was troubled. “Where have you laid him?” He asked. They said, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept. Some said, “See how He loved him!” Others asked whether the Man who had opened the eyes of the blind could not have kept this man from dying.

Groaning again, Jesus came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it. “Take away the stone,” He said. Martha objected, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus said, “Did I not say to you that if you would believe you would see the glory of God?” So they took away the stone. Jesus lifted up His eyes and said, “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me.” He said it aloud for the sake of those standing by, that they might believe the Father had sent Him.

Then He cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come forth!” And the dead man came out, bound hand and foot with graveclothes, his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Loose him, and let him go.” Many of those who had come to Mary and had seen what Jesus did believed in Him. But some went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

scene.label: Bethany
scene.text: A village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem (11:18). Going there meant coming within easy reach of the leaders who had just tried to stone Jesus, which is why Thomas expected to die.

scene.label: Four days
scene.text: If Jesus was near the Jordan, about a day’s journey away, the timeline probably ran like this: a day for the messenger, two days’ wait, a day’s walk. Lazarus likely died about the time the message reached Jesus. By the fourth day no one could doubt he was dead; Martha expected decay.

scene.label: Mourning
scene.text: Burial usually took place on the day of death, and mourning went on for days, with friends coming to sit with the family. Many came out from Jerusalem, which suggests the family was well known.

scene.label: The tomb
scene.text: Families who could afford it used tombs cut into the rock, with a stone across the entrance. The body was wrapped in strips of cloth with spices, and the face covered with a separate cloth (compare John 19:40; 20:7).

scene.label: Groaned and wept
scene.text: The word for “groaned” (vv. 33, 38) describes strong, stern emotion, even indignation; Mark uses it when Jesus “strictly warned” a healed leper (Mark 1:43). Mary and the mourners wept aloud in lament; the word for Jesus’ weeping means shedding tears.

witnesses.john: Only John records the raising of Lazarus. It is the last and greatest sign before the cross, and John shows its cost: the gift of life to Lazarus leads straight to the council’s decision to put Jesus to death (11:53). His note about Mary’s anointing (11:2), told later in chapter 12, suggests his readers already knew that story.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the resurrection and the life, not only on the last day but in person, standing at the tomb. He weeps with grieving friends, and then He speaks, and the dead man walks out.
seeing.living: Martha believed in a resurrection “at the last day.” Jesus moved her hope from an event to a Person, and then asked, “Do you believe this?” When He seems to come too late, He has not stopped loving you, and He still has the last word over death.
seeing.ponder: Where has Jesus seemed to come too late for you, and how would you answer Him if He asked, “Do you believe this?”

preaching.big_idea: Jesus is the resurrection and the life, and death must answer when He calls.
outline: A delay that served God’s glory (1–16)
A promise to a grieving sister (17–27)
A voice that wakes the dead (38–46)
preaching.watch_for: The word “believe” runs through the chapter (vv. 15, 25–27, 40, 42, 45), and so does “glory” (vv. 4, 40). John shows the delay, the tears and the open tomb all serving one aim: that people would see God’s glory and believe.

title: Lazarus Raised from the Dead
